title: One lost packet in HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
purpose: See at which layer head-of-line blocking happens in each HTTP version, and how ALPN picks the version.
sequence_reason: Each HTTP version fixes the blocking of the version before it, so the order of the versions and the effect of one lost packet are the idea.
summary: A page needs three files: A style.css, B app.js and C logo.png. HTTP/1.1 sends one request at a time per connection, so B and C wait behind A. HTTP/2 interleaves all three as frames on one TCP connection, but when one TCP packet is lost, TCP holds back every byte after the gap, so all three stall. HTTP/3 gives each request its own QUIC stream, and QUIC recovers loss per stream, so only A waits. The version is chosen with ALPN during the TLS handshake: the client offers names, the server picks one. A server advertises h3 with Alt-Svc, and clients fall back to TCP when UDP is blocked.
explanation: Head-of-line blocking moves down a layer with each version: HTTP/2 removes it from HTTP, and HTTP/3 removes it from the transport by using QUIC streams instead of one TCP byte stream.

learning_check.question: One packet that carries part of response A is lost. Which responses wait on HTTP/2 over TCP, and which on HTTP/3?
learning_check.answer: On HTTP/2 over TCP, A, B and C all wait, because TCP releases bytes only in order. On HTTP/3, only A waits, because each QUIC stream recovers its own loss.

scenes.heading: Three versions, one lost packet
scenes.narration: Three HTTP versions carry the same three files. Watch what one lost packet does in each version.

scenes.heading: Same meaning, new framing
scenes.narration: Methods, status codes and headers mean the same in every version. Only the framing and the transport change.

visual.verdict: Same semantics, different framing and transport.

scenes.heading: HTTP/1.1: one request at a time
scenes.narration: On one HTTP/1.1 connection, the browser sends GET A, waits for response A, and only then sends GET B.

path.label: Only now the browser sends GET B

scenes.heading: Head-of-line blocking in HTTP
scenes.narration: If response A is slow, B and C wait behind it. So browsers open several TCP connections per host instead.

items: B and C wait behind A
Browsers open several TCP connections per host

scenes.heading: HTTP/2: many streams, one TCP connection
scenes.narration: HTTP/2 splits messages into binary frames. Frames of streams A, B and C interleave on one TCP connection.

path.label: Requests A, B and C leave together as frames
Frames of the three streams interleave

scenes.heading: One lost TCP packet stalls every stream
scenes.narration: A TCP packet with a frame of A is lost. TCP delivers bytes only in order, so frames of B and C wait too.

items: A TCP packet with a frame of A is lost
Frames of B and C arrive after the gap
TCP holds every byte after the gap
A, B and C stall until the retransmission

scenes.heading: HTTP/3: one QUIC stream per request
scenes.narration: HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP. Each request gets its own QUIC stream: A on stream 0, B on 4, C on 8.

path.label: A on stream 0, B on stream 4, C on stream 8
Each stream is ordered on its own

scenes.heading: The same loss stalls only A
scenes.narration: On HTTP/3 over QUIC, the same lost packet delays only stream 0, response A. On HTTP/2 over TCP, all three waited.

scenes.heading: ALPN picks the version
scenes.narration: During the TLS handshake, the client offers protocol names with ALPN, such as h2 and http/1.1. The server picks one.

path.label: The client offers protocol names in TLS

scenes.heading: Finding HTTP/3 with Alt-Svc
scenes.narration: A server advertises h3 with the Alt-Svc header. The client opens QUIC with ALPN h3, and falls back to TCP if UDP is blocked.

items: The server sends the Alt-Svc header with h3
The client opens QUIC with ALPN h3
UDP is blocked: the client falls back to TCP
